Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: defendant officer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an officer's use of a taser on an actively resisting suspect does not violate clearly established Fourth Amendment law.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

## ARGUMENT

### The district court should have granted qualified immunity because no clearly established law forbade tasing an actively resisting suspect.

Qualified immunity protects an officer unless (1) the officer violated a constitutional right that (2) was clearly established at the time of the conduct. *Pearson v. Callahan*, 555 U.S. 223, 232 (2009). A right is clearly established only if its contours are "sufficiently clear that every reasonable official would have understood that what he is doing violates that right." *Mullenix v. Luna*, 577 U.S. 7, 11-12 (2015) (per curiam) (cleaned up). The Supreme Court has repeatedly warned against defining clearly established law "at a high level of generality," and it has stressed that the inquiry is especially demanding in the excessive-force context, where outcomes turn on specific facts. *Id.* at 12.

**A. This Court has consistently treated tasing as a reasonable response to active resistance.**

Under *Graham v. Connor*, 490 U.S. 386, 396 (1989), reasonableness turns on the severity of the crime, the threat to officers, and whether the suspect is actively resisting or fleeing. This Court has applied those factors to tasers many times, and the line it draws is whether the suspect was resisting. It has not drawn the line at the use of the device itself.

In *Rudlaff v. Gillispie*, 791 F.3d 638, 641-43 (6th Cir. 2015), this Court held that an officer who tased a suspect who was resisting arrest did not violate the Fourth Amendment. It stressed that the suspect's own noncompliance, not the officer's choice of tool, drove the analysis. Similarly, in *Hagans v. Franklin County Sheriff's Office*, 695 F.3d 505, 509-11 (6th Cir. 2012), this Court held that officers who tased a suspect who refused to comply with commands and continued to resist were entitled to qualified immunity. And in *Kent v. Oakland County*, 810 F.3d 384, 391-95 (6th Cir. 2016), the Court again recognized that officers may apply force proportionate to a detainee's continuing resistance without violating clearly established law.

**B. The decisions finding violations involve non-resisting suspects, which is the opposite of this case.**

The cases in which this Court has denied immunity for taser use confirm the distinction. In *Goodwin v. City of Painesville*, 781 F.3d 314, 322-29 (6th Cir. 2015), the Court held that tasing a suspect who was not resisting could violate clearly established law. It distinguished tasing a suspect who is actively resisting. *Austin v. Redford Township Police Department*, 690 F.3d 490, 498-99 (6th Cir. 2012), likewise rested on the suspect's having stopped resisting, because the clearly established right is to be free from gratuitous force once a suspect is subdued and compliant. And *Roell v. Hamilton County*, 870 F.3d 471, 483-89 (6th Cir. 2017), turned on the absence of any meaningful resistance by a restrained, non-threatening individual.

Those decisions mark the boundary of the clearly established right. Here, the record shows that Plaintiff [actively resisted by *describe specific conduct: pulling away, refusing to give hands, striking or grappling with officers, etc.*] before and at the moment the taser was deployed. The officer ceased [or did not continue] the taser cycle once Plaintiff stopped resisting. That sequence places this case on the *Rudlaff* and *Hagans* side of the line and outside the *Goodwin*, *Austin*, and *Roell* line.

**C. Plaintiff cannot identify controlling authority that put the unlawfulness of this conduct beyond debate.**

Plaintiff bears the burden of showing that the right was clearly established. To do so, he must identify a case with materially similar facts or show that the violation was so obvious that no precedent was needed. *District of Columbia v. Wesby*, 583 U.S. 48, 63-64 (2018). He can do neither. The decisions on which he relies concern suspects who had stopped resisting, were restrained, or were incapacitated. Given *Rudlaff* and *Hagans*, a reasonable officer confronting a suspect who was actively resisting could not have known that a taser deployment violated the Fourth Amendment. At most, the law was unsettled as applied to resisting suspects, and that is enough to compel qualified immunity.

Because no clearly established law prohibited the officer's use of a taser on an actively resisting suspect, the denial of qualified immunity should be reversed.
